ctx: A face-matching system for building entry rejects women with darker skin tones much more often than other employees.
q: Which responsible AI principle is most affected?
exp: When a system works worse for some groups than for others, those people receive a lower quality of service, which is a fairness harm. Transparency, accountability and privacy are important for such a system too, but the unequal error rate is the core problem described.

q: Complete the sentences about fairness.
tpl: When a model gives worse results for one group of people, this is a {0} issue. Checking metrics separately for each group is called {1} evaluation.
exp: Unequal results for different groups are a fairness issue. Disaggregated evaluation breaks metrics down by group so that gaps hidden by an overall average become visible. Aggregated metrics are exactly what can hide those gaps, and random evaluation is not a fairness method.

q: For each of the following statements about reliability and safety, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Tests for a driver-assistance system should include rare situations, such as heavy snow.
Reliability matters only for hardware, not for AI models.
A rollback plan helps when a new model version behaves badly.
exp: Yes for the first: rare but realistic conditions are where failures often appear. No for the second: AI models must behave consistently and safely too, which is the point of this principle. Yes for the third: being able to return to the previous version limits harm from a bad update.

q: What is the safest way to move all users of an AI app to a new model version?
opts: Switch everyone at once without testing
Evaluate the new version, roll it out gradually, monitor it and keep a way to roll back
Turn off monitoring during the change
exp: Evaluating first, releasing gradually and monitoring let you catch problems before they affect everyone, and a rollback path limits the damage if something goes wrong. Switching blindly, deleting the old version or turning off monitoring removes these safeguards.

ctx: A smart speaker records and uploads all room audio continuously, even when nobody has said the wake word.
q: Which responsible AI principle is the main concern?
exp: Collecting audio that users did not intend to share invades their privacy and creates security risks for that data. A responsible design processes only what is needed, for example by listening locally for the wake word and uploading audio only after it is spoken.

q: Match each practice to the privacy or security concept it represents. Each concept can be used once or not at all.
items: Collect only the fields the app needs
Ask users before using their data
Limit access to data with roles
exp: Encrypting stored data is encryption, collecting only needed fields is data minimization, asking users first is consent, and role-based limits are access control. Inclusive design is about accessibility, not about protecting data.

q: An app lets users choose between voice input and typed input. Which principle does this mainly support?
exp: Offering several ways to interact lets people with different abilities and preferences use the app, which is inclusiveness. Accountability concerns ownership, reliability concerns consistent and safe behavior, and fairness concerns equal outcomes.

q: For each of the following statements about inclusiveness, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Inclusive design can also benefit people without disabilities.
Testing only with the development team is enough to make an app inclusive.
Supporting several languages can make an app more inclusive.
exp: Yes for the first: features such as captions and voice control help many people, for example in noisy or hands-busy situations. No for the second: a small, similar group misses many barriers; diverse users should be involved. Yes for the third: language support lets more people use the app.

ctx: A card issuer's AI system automatically blocks cards when it suspects fraud. Customers are only told 'Your card is blocked.'
q: What change best supports transparency?
opts: Block more cards to be safe
Tell customers that an automated system flagged the transaction and how they can get it reviewed
exp: People affected by automated decisions should know that AI was involved and how to question the outcome. Explaining the automated flag and the review process supports transparency and also accountability. Blocking more cards, hiding reasons or changing the card design do not help customers understand the decision.

q: Which TWO items belong in the documentation of an AI system to support transparency? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
opts: Known limitations and situations where the system can fail
exp: Transparency documentation, such as a Transparency Note, explains what the system is for and where it can fail, so people use it appropriately. Personal addresses and passwords must never be published, and a menu has nothing to do with the AI system.

q: A team wants to use an existing AI system for a new purpose that it was not designed for. Who should decide whether this is allowed?
opts: The system's owners, after a responsible AI review of the new use
exp: New uses can bring new risks, so accountable owners should review them against the organization's responsible AI requirements before approving. Individual users and the model are not accountable, and allowing any use without review ignores the risks.

q: Complete the sentences about accountability.
tpl: Human {0} lets people review or override important AI decisions. An {1} trail records what the system did and when.
exp: Human oversight keeps people in control of important decisions, and an audit trail records actions so that outcomes can be investigated later. Temperature and quota are model settings, and color or random trails are not accountability mechanisms.

q: Which of the following is an output of generative AI?
exp: Generative AI creates new content, such as a drafted email. Sensor readings, row IDs and file sizes are recorded or calculated data, not content created by a model.

q: In generative AI, what is a transformer?
opts: A neural network architecture that uses attention and is the basis of most large language models
exp: The transformer is a neural network architecture built around attention, which lets the model weigh how tokens relate to each other; GPT and most modern language models use it. It is not a database, a piece of hardware or a billing plan.

q: For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A larger context window lets a model consider more text at once.
Every token costs the same amount in every model.
A model can explain its reasoning, but the explanation can still be wrong.
exp: Yes for the first: the context window limits how much input and output fit in one request. No for the second: prices differ by model and often between input and output tokens. Yes for the third: explanations are generated text too, so they can contain mistakes and should be checked.

q: Match each term to its description. Each description can be used once or not at all.
targets: The text that the model generates in response
The input you send to the model
Running a trained model to get an output
The learned weights inside a model
exp: Parameters are the learned weights, inference is running the trained model, the prompt is the input, and the completion is the generated output. The deployment region is a hosting setting and does not describe any of these terms.

q: Which TWO reasons explain why a language model can give a wrong answer? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
opts: It always checks a database before answering
It is connected to the live internet by default
Its training data can be outdated or incomplete
It predicts likely text instead of verifying facts
exp: Models learn from data with a cutoff and gaps, and they generate likely text rather than checking facts, so they can be confidently wrong. They do not check databases or the internet unless a solution adds those tools, and generation is based on probabilities.

q: Which type of model turns written text into natural-sounding speech?
exp: Text-to-speech models, and Azure Speech neural voices, convert text into spoken audio. Embedding models produce vectors, image-generation models create pictures, and classification models assign labels.

ctx: A company builds an internal tool that summarizes confidential documents. Company policy requires that processing stays within the EU.
q: Which deployment choice fits?
opts: A model offered with a Data Zone Standard deployment in the EU data zone
Any model with a Global Standard deployment
A model running on an employee's personal laptop without approval
exp: Data Zone deployments keep processing inside a defined zone such as the EU, which meets the policy while still providing managed capacity. Global Standard can process requests in any region, image models cannot summarize text, and unapproved personal devices break security policy.

q: For each of the following statements about model settings, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Temperature affects how focused or creative answers are.
Maximum tokens limits how long a response can be.
The deployment name changes how the model answers.
exp: Yes for the first: lower temperature gives focused answers, and higher gives more varied ones. Yes for the second: generation stops when the token limit is reached. No for the third: the deployment name is just an identifier for calling the model; it does not change its behavior.

q: Match each symptom to the setting that addresses it. Each setting can be used once or not at all.
items: Answers keep repeating the same phrase
Answers must end at the word STOP
Answers are cut off in the middle
exp: A frequency penalty reduces repetition, a stop sequence ends output at a chosen word, a lower temperature makes answers less random, and a higher max tokens value prevents cut-off answers. Changing the region does not affect the content of answers.

q: When you call a reasoning model, which parameter controls how much effort it spends thinking before it answers?
exp: Reasoning models accept a reasoning effort setting, such as low, medium or high, that trades answer quality on hard problems against time and token cost; many of them do not support sampling settings such as temperature. Presence penalty and stop sequences do not control reasoning depth.

q: Complete the sentences about choosing models.
tpl: For semantic search over documents, you deploy an {0} model. For a chatbot that reads screenshots that users upload, you deploy a {1} model.
exp: Embedding models turn text into vectors for meaning-based search, and multimodal models accept images such as screenshots along with text. Image-generation and speech models create pictures or audio, and embedding models cannot read screenshots or hold a conversation.

q: Which TWO statements describe a Global Standard deployment? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
opts: It uses Azure's global capacity, which gives higher default throughput
It guarantees processing inside one country
It provides reserved capacity billed per hour
You pay only for the tokens that you use
It returns results within a 24-hour batch window
exp: Global Standard routes requests across Azure's worldwide capacity and charges per token used. It does not keep processing inside one country, which is what Data Zone or regional types address, reserved hourly capacity describes Provisioned, and the 24-hour window describes Global Batch.

q: Put the steps for choosing a model for a new solution in the correct order. Not every step is used.
items: Test the shortlisted models with your own prompts and evaluations
Pick the model with the most interesting name
List the requirements, such as task, languages, input types and budget
Deploy the best model and monitor it
Shortlist models from the catalog by using model cards and benchmarks
exp: Start from the requirements, use model cards and benchmarks to build a shortlist, test the shortlist on your own data, and then deploy and monitor the winner. A model's name says nothing about whether it fits your requirements.

q: What is a tokens-per-minute (TPM) quota?
opts: The maximum number of tokens that a deployment can process per minute
The size of the model's context window
exp: TPM quota is a rate limit on how many tokens a deployment can handle each minute; requests beyond it are throttled. It is not a price, a user count or the context window, which limits the tokens in a single request.
